title: TS SDK streaming bridge cookbook: progressive consumption & resumable iterators
creator: Ava Patel
description: Create a practical cookbook and implementation for bidirectional conversion patterns between AsyncIterable<T> and Web Streams (ReadableStream) in the TypeScript SDK. Focus on progressive consumption (consume-first semantics), resumability after transient errors, cancellation semantics, and backpressure alignment between Node/Browser runtimes. Deliver a small set of exported helpers, robust examples, and tests demonstrating streaming retry and safe framing for tokenized / chunked model outputs.
acceptance_criteria: Provide two exported helpers: toAsyncIterable(stream) and toWebReadable(iterable)
Helpers correctly propagate cancel/abort signals from both sides (AbortController + iterator.return)
Demonstrate resumable consumption: restart from last safe frame boundary after a transient network error and continue decoding the rest of a response
Examples included for Node (native streams / WHATWG) and browser (ReadableStream) environments
Automated tests cover backpressure scenarios, double-consumption protection, and cancellation propagation
Doc page (Cookbook) with migration notes and recommended patterns for SDK consumers
technical_notes: Problem: Web Streams and AsyncIterator worlds expose different flow-control primitives; naive adapters can drop tokens or block forever under backpressure.
Design: adapters will use an internal buffer with bounded queue + promise-based flow-control to map ReadableStream.getReader().read() semantics to AsyncIterator.next() and vice-versa.

Resumability: require framing boundaries (newline/JSON-DELIM) for deterministic restart points. Where model outputs are free-form, provide a framing helper (frameChunks) that yields frame markers for safe checkpointing.
Retries: a consumer-visible retry hook will accept a resume token (lastFrameId) and call the API with a resume param; SDK will expose an example pattern and a minimal backoff helper.
Cancellation: use AbortSignal for Web Streams and call iterator.return() for AsyncIterator consumers. Ensure both paths notify the runtime to close underlying model streams to free capacity.
Edge cases: double-consume detection (throw a clear error if consumer tries to convert the same underlying stream twice).
Runtime differences: Node 18+ has WHATWG ReadableStream, but some environments use stream.Readable; include small compatibility shim and doc notes.
implementation_plan: Spike (1 day): prototype adapter using bounded queue and tests that simulate slow consumer/fast producer and vice-versa
Core impl (2 days): implement toAsyncIterable and toWebReadable with AbortSignal integration and type-safe generics T
Framing helpers (1 day): frameChunks, findLastBoundary utilities and small JSON-lines encoder/decoder
Resumability flow (1 day): sample resume token wiring and example server-side contract in examples folder
Docs/tests (1 day): cookbook doc, migration notes, unit + integration tests using node-fetch + local test server
test_plan: Unit: adapter queue semantics under 1000 permutations of producer/consumer sync/async delays
Integration: run example consumer against a local server that streams JSONL chunks and validate restart behavior after forced TCP reset
Property: invariants for cancellation propagation (AbortSignal triggers underlying close and iterator.return resolves)
CI: add a deterministic stress matrix job that runs the slow-producer/fast-consumer and fast-producer/slow-consumer scenarios
Cross-env: tests run in Node 18 and Chrome Headless to ensure browser ReadableStream compatibility
rollout_plan: Feature branch -> PR with unit + integration tests
Early dogfood: enable new helpers in internal example apps (console-playground, examples/streaming-resume)
Beta: mark helpers as experimental in SDK docs and gather feedback for 2 weeks
General availability: promote to stable and update migration guide if no major issues are found

notes_for_reviewers: Focus reviews on cancellation semantics and ownership: ensure we do not leave dangling readers that block runtime capacity.
Pay special attention to the framing helpers; incorrect framing semantics will make resumability unsafe for customers.
Prefer minimal additional runtime dependencies (no new big packages). Keep implementation under ~120 lines each helper where possible.
